The protection of employees' privacy is central to employee data protection. However, this protection must always be balanced against the employer's interest in information. **FAQ Employee Data Protection** Source: COMiCZ via Getty Images Here you will find information and answers to frequently asked questions about your rights in an employment relationship or application process. **General on Employee Data Protection** **Which employees is the BfDI responsible for?** The Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) is responsible for data protection supervision of federal public bodies, including employee data protection at these bodies. Numerous federal public corporations, institutions, and foundations also fall under the BfDI's data protection supervision, such as professional associations, many statutory health insurance funds, or scientific research institutions. The BfDI also supervises private companies owned by the federal government. These include, for example, Bundeswehr Fuhrpark Service GmbH, Bundesrepublik Deutschland - Finanzagentur GmbH, and many others. Employees in the sense of Section 26 (8) BDSG include, among others, salaried employees, federal civil servants, soldiers, and applicants. The BfDI's jurisdiction also extends to the remaining federal civil servants at the Post-Successor Companies and Deutsche Bahn.

The BfDI's jurisdiction also extends to the remaining federal civil servants at the Post-Successor Companies and Deutsche Bahn. **What is the legal situation for employee data protection?** There is currently no independent employee data protection act. The BfDI has long advocated for the creation of employee data protection regulations. The Conference of Independent Data Protection Authorities of the Federal Government and the States (DSK) has also been calling for an employee data protection act for many years (see, for example, resolutions of April 29, 2022, and May 11, 2023). The interdisciplinary advisory board for employee data protection, established by the BMAS, also concluded in its final report of January 2022 that – in addition to other measures – an independent employee data protection act is necessary. The currently applicable norm, which was enacted by the German legislator on the basis of the opening clause of Art. 88 GDPR for data processing in an employment context, is Section 26 BDSG. According to this, personal data of employees may be processed for purposes of the employment relationship, for example, if this is necessary for the decision on the establishment, execution, or termination of the employment relationship.

However, the current provision of Section 26 BDSG is insufficient in view of current legal (see in particular the judgment of the European Court of Justice (ECJ) of March 30, 2023, in case C-34/21) and technological developments (e.g., in artificial intelligence). The norm is too vague, leaves too much room for interpretation, is not sufficiently practical, norm-clear, or appropriate. As the digitalization of the working world enables increasingly extensive monitoring of employees and there is great interest in utilizing these technical possibilities, the need for employees and applicants for adequate protection of their right to informational self-determination is growing. Specific regulations for German employee data protection are required to ensure a proportionate balance between the constitutionally protected interests of employers and the right to informational self-determination of employees.

This means specific protective measures for data subjects, tailored to the respective processing situation. Such protective measures can be technical, organizational, or legal in nature. The mandate to create regulations on employee data protection, enshrined in the current coalition agreement, is to be implemented under the joint leadership of the BMI and the BMAS. It would be welcome if the project of creating an employee data protection act were completed in the current, 20th legislative period. Further specific provisions within the meaning of the GDPR can be found in numerous labor and service law statutes. The Occupational Safety and Health Act, the Maternity Protection Act, the General Equal Treatment Act, the Social Code Book Nine, or the Remuneration Transparency Act, and not least the Federal Civil Servants Act (BBG) or the Federal Staff Representation Act, are just a small selection of the numerous legal bases that entail the processing of personal data in the employment context.

These special federal data protection regulations take precedence over the general data protection regulations of the BDSG. **Can consent be given in an employment relationship?** According to Art. 6 (1) lit. a), Art. 7 GDPR in conjunction with Section 26 (2) BDSG, the processing of personal data in an employment relationship can also be based on consent. A mandatory prerequisite here is that consent is given in an informed manner and is actually voluntary. Whether this actual voluntariness exists must be assessed according to the circumstances of the individual case. In doing so, the fundamentally existing dependency of the employee on the employer in the employment relationship must be taken into account. If, for example, an employee should refuse a video recording of themselves during participation in an event of their employer, no disadvantages may arise for them from this, and their participation in the event must still be possible. A legal or economic advantage that the employee gains through the declaration of consent also speaks in favor of voluntariness, e.g., when introducing a company health system or permission for private use of company IT systems.

Persons who apply are considered employees according to Section 26 (8) sentence 2 BDSG. If an employment relationship comes about after an application, the necessary application documents are added to the personnel file. **Application by email or online** Applications are sent conventionally by post as well as by email or electronically. When sending by email, it should be noted that data transmission is often not protected, so encryption should be used. If an application by email is possible, the employer must allow an equivalent, e.g., postal, application. The possibility of only being able to apply by email is therefore not sufficient. If the employer offers applications via internet platforms with online input masks, the processing must be protected by appropriate technical and organizational measures.

Voluntary consent is required not only from the applicants but also from the interview partners on the employer's side. For applicants, consent is only voluntary if they are also offered a personal interview or a telephone conversation as an alternative. In time-delayed interviews, the answers to displayed questions are recorded and later evaluated. This type of interview also allows for the evaluation of non-verbal behavior or the use of speech analysis procedures. In these methods, the questions of suitability, necessity, and proportionality arise under data protection law. Furthermore, particular attention must be paid to limiting access possibilities and timely deletion of the recording. **Data protection-compliant questions in the application process** In the application process, only those questions may be asked that are relevant to the specific job. In this context, therefore, only data may be processed for which the employer has a legitimate, justifiable, and worthy interest in a truthful answer, so that the applicant's concerns must take a back seat to these.

Personnel files include all data concerning employees, insofar as it is directly related to the employment relationship (personnel file data). Regulations on the data protection-compliant handling of personnel file data can be found primarily in Sections 106 et seq. BBG. Unless collective agreements contain specific provisions, the civil service regulations also apply to collectively agreed employees. For soldiers, Sections 29 et seq. of the Soldiers Act apply. The legal provisions are concretized in personnel file guidelines, e.g., of the BMI. Personnel file data also includes data stored in files (e.g., in a human resources information system).

Unofficial files, as are often kept by supervisors, are inadmissible! * Personnel file data may only be used for purposes of personnel administration or human resources management. * Personnel files must be stored in such a way that unauthorized access is excluded. * Only employees who are involved in the processing of personnel matters within the framework of personnel administration may have access to personnel files. * Employees have a right to inspect their complete personnel file. Excerpts, copies, or photocopies may be made. Printouts from human resources information systems are also possible. The right of inspection is part of the broader right of access according to Art. 15 GDPR. * Personnel files may only be forwarded to other authorities with the consent of the employee. Exceptions to this are regulated by law (e.g., Section 111 (1) BBG, Section 29 (1) BDG).

As a rule, only employees entrusted with processing personnel matters may access it, and only insofar as this is necessary for purposes of personnel administration or human resources management. The legislator has granted equal opportunities officers access to decision-relevant parts of the personnel file and thus also to automatically stored personnel file data. However, this only applies insofar as access is necessary for the performance of tasks under the Federal Equal Opportunities Act. Its processing is only permitted under certain conditions. In connection with an employment relationship, these are primarily cases where the processing of health data is necessary for exercising rights and fulfilling obligations arising from an illness or a severe disability. These can be rights and obligations of both the employee and the employer. Health data includes, for example, health certificates and medical opinions on health suitability. The result is sent in a separate and sealed envelope and sealed and added to the personnel file. **Illness and sick leave** The recording of incapacity for work due to illness has various aspects. It is necessary and thus permissible under data protection law for the fulfillment of legal provisions, e.g., for calculating the duration of continued wage payment or for making an offer for a measure of company integration management (BEM). These tasks are incumbent on the employer, so only the personnel administration may and must carry out data processing for this purpose.

The procedure aims to identify the causes of incapacity for work and jointly seek a way to avoid or reduce future periods of incapacity for work. In this procedure, data on illnesses are regularly processed as sensitive data within the meaning of Art. 9 GDPR.

However, supervisors may process personal data of their employees within the framework of their leadership role if this is necessary for the following purposes: **Work organization and personnel management** From a data protection perspective, there are no objections if supervisors use personal information about their employees insofar as this is necessary for the organizational and personnel management of the respective organizational unit. For example, the head of an organizational unit can record in writing work assignments given to a person and deadlines with regard to managing task completion. **Absence lists** Among the organizational tasks of a supervisor is also the maintenance of an absence and vacation plan.

In this data processing and its control by the employer, the employees' right to informational self-determination and the employer's interest in complying with codes of conduct must be weighed against each other. Employers have a legitimate interest in preventing abuse or even criminal acts when using the company's internet access. Therefore, the employer may monitor the browsing behavior of its employees. However, a timely evaluation of log data, whether as a sample or possibly in connection with a specific suspicion of abuse, is permissible. The control of employees' browsing activities is possible via so-called system logs. Demnach haben Fachvorgesetzte keinen Zugang zu Personalaktendaten ihrer Mitarbeitenden. Ebenso dürfen in den Fachabteilungen keine Personalteil- oder Personalnebenakten geführt werden. So kann die Leitung einer Organisationseinheit im Hinblick auf die Steuerung der Aufgabenerledigung beispielsweise einer Person erteilten Arbeitsaufträge und terminliche Vorgaben schriftlich festhalten. BfDI Guidance - BfDI - Smartwatches for Children

Smartwatches for Children Children today grow up in a digitized environment. For older children who are not yet allowed to own a smartphone, there are simple smartwatch models available as a stylish alternative. The market offers a variety of models with different functionalities – from simple calling to a complete smartphone replacement. In this section, you will find information on the operation, functions, and data transmission of smartwatches. You will also find tips for data-minimizing use of a smartwatch. Data Transmission with a Smartwatch A smartwatch does not transmit data directly to the parents' smartphone. Often, not only the manufacturer but sometimes also third-party providers are involved in between. This can become a problem, especially with sensitive location data. Learn more: Data transmission with a smartwatch The Smartwatch and its Functions A smartwatch has many functions that are in no way inferior to those of modern smartphones. This has implications for your child's data protection. However, you can influence many things through the settings. Learn more: The smartwatch and its functions Operation and Settings of a Smartwatch There are also different options for the everyday operation of a child's smartwatch. Models differ even in how they are turned on and off. The question of who may call the child can also be configured. Some of these are also relevant for good data protection.
